title: Power Sharing
summary: This chapter explores power sharing mechanisms in democracies, analyzing different forms like horizontal, vertical, and political power sharing. It examines case studies of Belgium and Sri Lanka to illustrate successful and failed approaches to power sharing. The chapter discusses the prudential and moral reasons for power sharing, different federal structures (coming-together and holding-together), and the significance of decentralization. It also addresses challenges like communalism, caste politics, gender inequality, and issues within political parties such as lack of internal democracy and dynastic succession. The analysis concludes by examining the characteristics of accountable, responsive, and legitimate governments.

sections.heading: Power Sharing in Belgium
sections.para: Belgium successfully addresses its diversity through power sharing. The country has a population divided into Dutch-speaking Flemish and French-speaking Walloians, along with a small German-speaking community. Belgium adopted a special system of government to accommodate these communities. The government is structured in a way that no single community can dominate others. The constitution prescribes that the number of Dutch and French-speaking ministers shall be equal. Many powers of the central government have been given to state governments of the two regions. Brussels has a separate government where both communities have equal representation. This power sharing arrangement helped Belgium avoid civic conflict.
points: Belgium has a population divided into Dutch-speaking Flemish and French-speaking Walloians
The constitution mandates equal representation of Dutch and French-speaking ministers
Brussels has a separate government with equal representation for both communities
Many central government powers have been devolved to regional governments
Power sharing helped Belgium avoid civic conflict despite linguistic diversity
The Belgian model demonstrates successful accommodation of diversity

keyTerms.meaning: Division of population based on language and cultural differences

sections.trick: Remember Belgium's power sharing as 'Equal Languages, Equal Power' - both Dutch and French communities get equal representation in government.
sections.examPointer: CBSE often asks 2-mark questions on Belgium's power sharing mechanism and 4-mark questions comparing it with Sri Lanka. Focus on constitutional provisions and community representation.

sections.heading: Majoritarianism in Sri Lanka
sections.para: Sri Lanka presents a contrasting case where the Sinhala community sought to dominate other communities. The democratically elected government adopted a series of majoritarian policies to establish Sinhala supremacy. In 1956, an Act was passed to recognize Sinhala as the only official language. The constitution provided special position to Buddhism, favoring Sinhala applicants for university positions and government jobs. These policies alienated the Tamil community, who felt that their interests and identity were being ignored. The distrust between the two communities turned into a civil conflict that continued for about 30 years. The Sri Lankan experience shows that the rule of the majority is not always just and can threaten the unity of the country.

Sinhala was recognized as the only official language in 1956
Buddhism was given special status in the constitution

sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently asks 3-mark questions on Sri Lanka's majoritarian policies and 5-mark questions comparing it with Belgium's power sharing. Focus on specific policies and their consequences.

sections.heading: Forms of Power Sharing
sections.para: Power sharing can be understood in different ways. At the horizontal level, power is shared among different organs of government such as legislature, executive, and judiciary. This is known as checks and balances. At the vertical level, power is shared between different levels of government - central, state, and local. Political power sharing involves power sharing among various social groups such as religious and linguistic groups. In a democracy, power sharing is valuable as it reduces the possibility of conflict between social groups. It also ensures that the views of all sections of society are represented in governance. Power sharing is not just desirable but essential for the functioning of a democracy.
points: Horizontal power sharing: among different organs of government
Vertical power sharing: among different levels of government
Political power sharing: among different social groups
Power sharing reduces the possibility of conflict
It ensures representation of all social groups
Power sharing is essential for democratic functioning

sections.trick: Remember the three forms of power sharing as 'Three L's': Legislative, Local, and Linguistic groups.
sections.examPointer: CBSE asks 2-3 mark questions on different forms of power sharing. Be prepared to distinguish between horizontal and vertical power sharing with examples.

sections.heading: Prudential and Moral Reasons for Power Sharing
sections.para: Power sharing is valuable for both prudential and moral reasons. Prudential reasons suggest that power sharing will bring better outcomes. It reduces the possibility of conflict and leads to stability in the political system. Power sharing ensures that all communities have a stake in the country and are more likely to cooperate with each other. Moral reasons emphasize that power sharing is the very spirit of democracy. Power sharing is good in itself as it respects diversity and accommodates different social groups. It is the expression of the fundamental belief that all citizens are equal and should be able to participate in governance. Both prudential and moral reasons make a strong case for power sharing in democracies.

sections.examPointer: CBSE asks 3-mark questions on prudential and moral reasons for power sharing. Be prepared to explain both with examples and their significance in democracies.

sections.heading: Federalism in India
sections.para: India has a federal system with a unitary bias. The Indian Constitution provides for a three-tier system of government - Union, State, and Local. The Union List contains subjects on which only the central government can make laws, including defense, foreign affairs, and currency. The State List contains subjects on which only state governments can make laws, including police and public order. The Concurrent List contains subjects on which both central and state governments can make laws, including education and forests. The distribution of powers is not strictly followed due to the central tendency in the system. The central government can override state governments in certain situations. The Indian federal system has evolved over time to accommodate regional aspirations and maintain national unity.

Three-tier government: Union, State, and Local

sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently asks 2-mark questions on the three lists and 4-5 mark questions on the federal structure of India. Focus on the distribution of powers and the unitary bias.

sections.heading: Types of Federations
sections.para: Federations can be classified into two types: coming-together federations and holding-together federations. Coming-together federations are formed by independent states coming together on their own to form a bigger unit. The central government tends to be more powerful in such federations. Examples include the United States of America, Switzerland, and Australia. Holding-together federations are formed when a large country decides to divide its power between the central and state governments. The state governments tend to be more powerful in such federations. India is an example of a holding-together federation. The central government often has more powers in holding-together federations to maintain national unity. The type of federation depends on historical circumstances and the need to accommodate diversity.

sections.heading: Decentralization After 1992
sections.para: The 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments in 1992 marked a significant step towards decentralization in India. The 73rd Amendment established Panchayati Raj institutions in rural areas, while the 74th Amendment established municipalities in urban areas. These institutions have been given constitutional status and are now mandatory in all states. The amendments reserved one-third of seats for women in these bodies. They also reserved seats for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population. The State Election Commissions were created to conduct regular elections to these institutions. The local governments now have been given powers and responsibilities in several areas, including preparation of plans for economic development and social justice. These reforms have strengthened grassroots democracy and made governance more responsive to local needs.

sections.heading: Gender Division of Labour
sections.para: Gender division of labour refers to the division of work based on gender roles. In most societies, women are expected to do the housework and take care of children, while men are expected to work outside and earn money. This division is not natural but socially constructed. The sexual division of labour reinforces the idea that women are naturally suited for doing housework while men are suited for working outside. This division has serious consequences for women. It limits their opportunities for education and employment. It also creates inequality between men and women in the family and society. Feminist movements have challenged this division and demanded equal rights and opportunities for women. The struggle for gender equality continues in many parts of the world.

sections.heading: Communalism and Secularism
sections.para: Communalism is a belief that people belonging to the same religious community have common secular interests, which are different from the interests of those belonging to other religious communities. It involves using religious identity for political purposes and promoting the interests of one's own religious community at the expense of others. Communalism can take various forms from mild to extreme. It can lead to social tension and conflict. Secularism is the opposite of communalism. It involves treating all religions equally and ensuring that the state does not favor any particular religion. In India, secularism means that the state maintains a distance from religion and does not interfere in religious matters. It also ensures that all religions are treated equally by the state. Secularism is essential for maintaining harmony in a diverse society.

sections.examPointer: CBSE frequently asks 3-mark questions on communalism and secularism and 5-mark questions on their relationship. Focus on definitions and examples in Indian context.

sections.heading: Caste in Politics
sections.para: Caste plays a significant role in Indian politics. Political parties often take caste into account when forming election strategies and making policies. Caste is used to mobilize voters and gain political support. In some cases, political representation has been given to castes that have been historically marginalized, such as Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes. This has helped in their political empowerment. However, caste politics can also lead to casteism, which is the practice of discriminating against people based on their caste. It can create divisions in society and hinder national unity. The relationship between caste and politics is complex. While caste-based mobilization has helped marginalized groups gain political voice, it has also reinforced caste identities and sometimes perpetuated caste divisions.

sections.heading: Challenges to Political Parties
sections.para: Political parties in India face several challenges. Lack of internal democracy is a major challenge where decisions are made by a few leaders without proper consultation with party members. Dynastic succession is another challenge where leadership positions are passed within families rather than being open to all. Money and muscle power play a significant role in politics, with wealthy individuals and criminals having undue influence. Political parties often lack transparency in their functioning and financial dealings. There is a lack of meaningful choice for voters as most parties have similar ideologies and policies. The election system is expensive, which limits the participation of common citizens. Despite these challenges, political parties remain essential for democratic functioning as they provide political leadership and represent diverse interests.

sections.heading: Characteristics of Democratic Government
sections.para: A democratic government is characterized by accountability, responsiveness, and legitimacy. Accountability means that the government is answerable to the people for its actions and decisions. If the government fails to fulfill its responsibilities, the people can vote it out of power in the next election. Responsiveness means that the government is sensitive to the needs and expectations of the people. It takes into account public opinion while making decisions. Legitimacy means that the government has the right to rule because it has been elected by the people through free and fair elections. A legitimate government commands the respect and support of the people. Economic growth and inequality are also important considerations. While economic growth is necessary for development, it must be accompanied by reduction in inequality to ensure that all sections of society benefit. Dignity and freedom are fundamental values that a democratic government must uphold for all citizens.

boardQuestions.question: Explain any three forms of power sharing.
boardQuestions.answer: Three forms of power sharing are: 1) Horizontal power sharing: It involves distribution of power among different organs of government such as legislature, executive and judiciary. Each organ checks the other to maintain balance of power. 2) Vertical power sharing: It involves distribution of power among different levels of government - central, state and local. It can be coming-together or holding-together federations. 3) Community power sharing: It involves giving political power to different communities based on language, religion or region. It helps in reducing conflict and promoting unity.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the majoritarianism in Sri Lanka and its consequences.
boardQuestions.answer: Majoritarianism in Sri Lanka refers to the dominance of the Sinhala community over other communities, especially the Tamils. In 1956, the government passed an Act to recognize Sinhala as the only official language. This was a majoritarian measure as it disregarded the interests of the Tamil community who spoke other languages. The government also followed a preferential policy that favored Sinhala applicants for university positions and government jobs. These measures led to deep resentment among the Tamils who felt that they were being denied equal rights and opportunities. This eventually led to the emergence of militant groups and a prolonged civil war in Sri Lanka. The consequences of majoritarianism include ethnic conflict, loss of lives, displacement of people and economic instability. It also led to international criticism and intervention.

boardQuestions.question: What is decentralisation? Explain the steps taken for decentralisation in India after 1992.
boardQuestions.answer: Decentralisation is the process of transferring power and decision-making authority from central government to local governments or communities. It brings decision-making closer to the people and promotes local self-governance. After 1992, several steps were taken for decentralisation in India: 1) 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments: These amendments established the third tier of government in the form of Panchayati Raj institutions in rural areas and Municipalities in urban areas. 2) Reservation for women: One-third of seats were reserved for women in Panchayats and Municipalities to increase their participation in local governance. 3) Transfer of funds: Central and state governments transfer funds to local bodies for carrying out development works. 4) Transfer of functions: Several functions like primary education, primary health care, etc. were transferred to local bodies. 5) Regular elections: Elections to local bodies are held regularly to ensure continuity of local self-governance.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the different types of lists in the Indian Constitution.
boardQuestions.answer: The Indian Constitution has three lists that specify the subjects on which laws can be made by the central and state governments: 1) Union List: Contains subjects on which only the central government can make laws. These include defence, foreign affairs, currency, banking, etc. 2) State List: Contains subjects on which only state governments can make laws. These include police, public health, agriculture, etc. 3) Concurrent List: Contains subjects on which both central and state governments can make laws. These include education, marriage, divorce, etc. In case of conflict, the central law prevails. 4) Residuary List: Contains subjects that are not mentioned in any of the three lists. Only the central government can make laws on these subjects.

boardQuestions.question: What is feminism? Explain the feminist movement in India.
boardQuestions.answer: Feminism is a collection of movements and ideologies aimed at defining, establishing and defending equal political, economic, social and cultural rights for women. It opposes the patriarchal norms and practices that discriminate against women. The feminist movement in India has been active since the 19th century and has focused on various issues like women's education, property rights, voting rights, etc. The movement has been led by both men and women and has taken various forms including social reform movements, women's organizations, political movements, etc. Some of the key issues addressed by the feminist movement in India include: 1) Gender equality in education and employment 2) Equal rights to property 3) Prevention of violence against women 4) Reservation for women in legislatures 5) Recognition of women's unpaid work in households. The movement has achieved significant success including the enactment of laws like the Dowry Prohibition Act, Domestic Violence Act, etc. However, gender discrimination continues to exist in various forms in Indian society.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the challenges to political parties in India.
boardQuestions.answer: Political parties in India face several challenges that affect their functioning and effectiveness. The main challenges are: 1) Lack of internal democracy: Many parties do not hold internal elections regularly and decisions are taken by a small group of leaders. This reduces the participation of ordinary members in decision-making. 2) Dynastic succession: In many parties, leadership positions are passed from one generation to the next within a family. This limits opportunities for new leaders and can lead to nepotism. 3) Money and muscle power: Many parties rely on wealthy candidates and criminals who can fund their campaigns and use their influence to win elections. This undermines the democratic process. 4) Lack of meaningful choices: Often, the policies of different parties are similar, making it difficult for voters to choose between them. 5) Regionalism: Some parties focus only on regional issues and ignore national issues, which can lead to fragmentation of the political system. These challenges need to be addressed to strengthen the democratic process in India.

boardQuestions.question: What is secularism? Explain how secularism is practiced in India.
boardQuestions.answer: Secularism is the principle of separation of religion from civic affairs and the state. It implies that the state will not promote or discriminate against any religion and all religions will be treated equally. In India, secularism is practiced in the following ways: 1) No state religion: India does not have a state religion. All religions are treated equally by the state. 2) Freedom of religion: The Constitution guarantees freedom of religion to all citizens. This includes the freedom to practice, profess and propagate religion. 3) No religious instruction: The state cannot provide religious instruction in any educational institution maintained by it. 4) Social reform: The state can interfere in religious matters to promote social reforms like abolition of untouchability, child marriage, etc. 5) Equal protection of laws: All citizens are equally protected by the laws of the state regardless of their religion. However, the state can make special provisions for the advancement of any socially and educationally backward classes of citizens, including Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the relationship between caste and politics in India.
boardQuestions.answer: Caste and politics in India are closely related. Political parties often use caste identities to mobilize voters. This has both positive and negative effects. On the positive side, it has led to the political empowerment of lower castes who were historically marginalized. Many political leaders from lower castes have emerged and have advocated for the rights of their communities. Reservation in educational institutions and government jobs has been extended to Other Backward Classes (OBCs) based on caste identities. This has helped in reducing social and economic inequalities. On the negative side, caste politics has led to fragmentation of society along caste lines. It has also led to vote bank politics where parties cater to the interests of particular castes to win elections. This can undermine national unity and development. Moreover, caste identities often override other identities like national or regional identities. Despite these challenges, caste continues to be an important factor in Indian politics and will remain so in the foreseeable future.

boardQuestions.question: What is communalism? Explain how communalism can be prevented.
boardQuestions.answer: Communalism is a social and political ideology that promotes the interests of a particular religious community over others. It involves religious discrimination, prejudice and conflict. Communalism can be prevented through the following measures: 1) Education: Educating people about different religions and promoting inter-faith harmony can help in reducing communalism. 2) Secularism: Promoting secular values and ensuring equal treatment of all religions by the state can prevent communalism. 3) Media: Responsible reporting by media can help in reducing communal tensions and promoting communal harmony. 4) Civil society: Civil society organizations can play an important role in promoting communal harmony and preventing communal violence. 5) Legal measures: Strict enforcement of laws against communal violence and hate speech can deter communal elements. 6) Political leadership: Political leaders should avoid making communal statements and should promote national unity. 7) Economic development: Economic development and reducing inequalities can help in reducing communal tensions as economic factors often contribute to communalism.

boardQuestions.question: Explain the features of a legitimate government.
boardQuestions.answer: A legitimate government has the following features: 1) Elected through free and fair elections: The government should be elected by the people through free and fair elections where every citizen has the right to vote and stand for election. 2) Respects fundamental rights: The government should respect and protect the fundamental rights of all citizens as guaranteed by the Constitution. 3) Accountable to the people: The government should be accountable to the people and should be answerable for its actions and decisions. 4) Transparent: The government should function transparently and provide information to the citizens about its functioning. 5) Responsive: The government should be responsive to the needs and preferences of the people and should take decisions accordingly. 6) Represents all sections: The government should represent all sections of society and should not discriminate against any section based on religion, caste, gender, etc.
